name: Spanish America
title: Social Hierarchy of Spanish America: From Viceroy to Enslaved
period: c. 1650–1800 (the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru)

tiers.name: The viceroy
tiers.you: You govern in the king’s name, command his armed forces and oversee the Church, but the judges of the Audiencia can write to Spain without your leave, and a public inquiry into your conduct awaits you when your term ends.
tiers.kid: The viceroy ruled New Spain or Peru for the king of Spain, who never crossed the ocean to visit.
tiers.rise: The king chose viceroys from the Spanish nobility, the army and the higher clergy, often after service elsewhere in the empire: Manuel de Amat y Junyent governed Chile before he became viceroy of Peru in 1761. The post ended with recall, death or the end of the term.
tiers.why: No Spanish king ever visited his American kingdoms.

tiers.name: Spanish-born Spaniards
tiers.you: You came from Spain, perhaps as a royal official or as a young clerk in a kinsman’s business; the crown trusts you with its highest offices, and the American-born resent you as a gachupín.
tiers.kid: Spaniards born in Spain held most of the top jobs in the colonies, as judges, bishops and royal officials.
tiers.rise: A Spaniard became a peninsular by sailing to the Indies with the crown’s licence, meant only for Catholics who could show they had no Jewish or Muslim ancestors. His children born in America were criollos.
tiers.why: Spaniards born in Spain, the peninsulares, were a small minority who held most of the highest offices.

tiers.name: American-born Spaniards
tiers.you: You were born in America to a Spanish family: you pay no tribute and may study, be ordained or sit on the town council, but the highest posts usually go to men born in Spain, and your family may own an hacienda or work as artisans.
tiers.kid: Criollos were people of Spanish families born in America; some were rich landowners and many were craftsmen or clerks.
tiers.rise: Birth to Spanish parents made a criollo, but so, in practice, could wealth and a Spanish way of life: the child of a castizo and a Spaniard counted as Spanish, and prosperous families paid to obscure a mixed ancestry. A criollo family that lost its fortune kept its legal status but could sink into poverty.
tiers.why: Spaniards born in the Americas, the criollos, formed the largest privileged group.

tiers.name: The clergy
tiers.term: clero secular (parish priests), clero regular (friars), monjas (nuns)
tiers.you: You serve the Church as a priest, friar or nun: church courts rather than royal ones try you, and you may live on Masses your family endowed for its dead.
tiers.kid: Priests, friars and nuns ran the churches, schools and hospitals of Spanish America.
tiers.rise: Sons of Spanish families, and some mestizos, entered the priesthood through the seminaries and universities; daughters entered convents with a dowry. The highest posts went mostly to men born in Spain, and the Bourbon reforms kept criollos further from them.
tiers.why: The Catholic Church reached into every town, and its clergy formed an estate of their own.
people: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

tiers.name: Indigenous nobles
tiers.term: caciques, cacicas, principales (New Spain); kurakas, curacas (Peru)
tiers.you: You are a cacique or kuraka, addressed as don or doña: you pay no tribute and may ride a horse and carry a sword, but you must collect your town’s tribute and send its men to the labour drafts.
tiers.kid: Indigenous nobles kept their titles under Spanish rule and governed their own towns for the king.
tiers.rise: Rank came by descent, proved in genealogies before Spanish courts, but the colonial authorities could also favour a compliant rival over the rightful heir. After the rebellion of 1780–1781 the crown stopped recognising many kurakas and banned the dress and emblems of the Inca nobility.
tiers.why: Spanish rule rested on the Indigenous nobility.

tiers.name: Mestizos
tiers.you: Your ancestors were Spanish and Indigenous: you pay no tribute and may carry a weapon with a licence, but the law forbids you to live in an Indigenous town, and officials class people like you with vagabonds.
tiers.kid: Mestizos had both Spanish and Indigenous ancestors, and unlike Indigenous people they paid no tribute to the king.
tiers.rise: An Indigenous villager who learned Spanish, lived as a mestizo and moved to a town could be recorded as one and so escape tribute; a mestizo family that married Spaniards could, in two generations, be written down as Spanish.
tiers.why: Mestizos, the descendants of Spaniards and Indigenous people, were the first and the most favoured of the castas, the people of mixed descent.

tiers.name: Indigenous commoners
tiers.you: You farm your community’s land and pay the king’s tribute; your town may be ordered to send men to the mines, but you can take your grievances to a royal court.
tiers.kid: Most people were Indigenous farmers who lived in their own towns and paid a yearly tax to the king of Spain.
tiers.rise: Moving to a Spanish town, estate or mine, learning Spanish and passing as a mestizo could free a man from tribute and the labour draft; a few proved noble descent in court and joined the nobility.
tiers.why: Most people were Indigenous commoners, legally free vassals of the king, grouped in the república de indios.

tiers.name: Free people of African descent
tiers.you: You are free, of African descent: you pay tribute, answer to the Inquisition and cannot be ordained, but you can work as an artisan, buy land and serve in a militia company of your own.
tiers.kid: Many people of African descent in Spanish America were free and worked as craftsmen, shopkeepers and soldiers.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by purchase, an owner’s grant or birth to a free mother. After that a skilled trade, militia service, wealth and marriage could raise a family, and some descendants were recorded as mestizos or even Spaniards.
tiers.why: By the 17th century free people of African descent outnumbered the enslaved in New Spain, and by 1800 they were about one person in ten there.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.term: esclavos; bozales (born in Africa), ladinos (Spanish-speaking), criollos (born in the colonies)
tiers.you: You belong to an owner who can sell you and keep your children, but the law lets you marry in church, keep savings and buy your freedom in instalments, as many do in the towns.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; many saved money to buy their freedom.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by purchase, often in instalments, by an owner’s grant in life or in a will, or by flight; a child followed its mother’s status, so a free mother’s children were born free.
tiers.why: From the 16th century some 200,000 enslaved Africans reached New Spain and some 95,000 Peru, by modern estimates, many under the asiento contracts the crown sold to foreign traders.
